The wars waged in the name of 9/11 have taken five times more American lives than were lost that day, not to mention set into motion events that led to the deaths of at least 4.5 million other people in the region and displaced 38 million more. They created more terrorists, more crises, more reasons for the United States to spend more lives and money on the latest military adventure — most famously in Iraq, where the US invasion produced the bloody Islamic State (ISIS) insurgency a decade later, and years of more US bombing, special forces operations, and proxy battles to beat it back. It’s been an especially dismal failure in North Africa, where terrorism has, ironically, exploded 100,000 percent since the US military started “fighting terror” there.Those who warned that the attacks themselves had been blowback for decades of elite-run US foreign policy in the first place were immediately shouted down, labeled traitors and terrorist-sympathizers. It took decades for this point to be metabolized and allowed to be uttered, as it is today even in the pages of conservative magazines. It was a shame that it did: closing off debate meant that, for years, US politicians responded to the attack by pursuing the exact same policies that made it more likely, further endangering innocent Americans.Not surprisingly, the anti-Americanism that so horrifically manifested in the attack is now arguably worse than ever. Washington has firmly lost the Arab world, and dozens of countries view China more positively, with the United States seen increasingly as a threat. Just like twenty-five years ago, the future costs of this global resentment likely won’t be borne by the Washington officials who put this bloodshed and mayhem into motion but by the ordinary Americans in whose name it’s been carried out — almost always without their input, approval, or even knowledge.Anti-American sentiment isn’t the only thing that’s gotten worse. Just as a chorus of Cassandras warned all those years ago, the war on terror that George W. Bush put into motion and every one of his predecessors escalated has become radically more lawless and extreme, while embedding itself menacingly deeper into Americans’ daily lives.American manufacturing shows little sign of coming back, but the US government has reshored the airborne assassination program it once exclusively reserved for Africa and the Middle East. The US president now claims the right to blast random fishing boats in international waters off the coast of the Americas on a whim, killing more than two hundred people and counting. Bush once upon a time went to Congress to get constitutional sign-off for his preemptive Middle East war. If he was in the White House now, he wouldn’t have to bother; the president can simply start one at will by assassinating a foreign head of state in a sneak attack on his home.Islamophobia has arguably never been more extreme in public life, even as the perpetrators of political violence are overwhelmingly right-wing American men. Members of Congress wallow in overt anti-Muslim bigotry that Bush and his class of Republicans never countenanced even as they waded waist-deep in Arab blood. Liberal and centrist commentators warn darkly of a sinister alliance between leftists and Muslims that threatens Western civilization, plundering the talking points of Weimar-era fascists who warned that communists were teaming up with a different religious minority. New York City commemorates today after a weeks-long controversy about its Muslim mayor attending, a racist narrative that seeped beyond the borders of right-wing media and into the pages of liberal outlets.“Terrorist” no longer refers to someone who blows up buildings or kills to make a political point, but that doesn’t mean the term has become meaningless. Instead it’s become a catch-all political slur for various nonviolent domestic political enemies: someone who vandalizes a billionaire megadonor’s car; who criticizes capitalism; who protests government policies or videotapes law enforcement; who simply moves a box of political zines; who wields political power while Muslim.The post–September 11 security state has turned firmly inward, with enormous public resources expended to root out, surveil, and prosecute political opponents as “terrorists.” The bloated Department of Homeland Security created in the attack’s aftermath sees itself explicitly as fighting a literal war against enemies within.What’s remarkable is that this is happening at the exact time the original fears and threats that justified it all are apparently no longer relevant.Firm evidence of Saudi complicity in 9/11 is only a few years old, but the US-Saudi relationship has somehow grown closer since: the president’s son-in-law inks multimillion-dollar deals with its government, the White House reflexively backs the country’s latest military adventures, and the president is now actively taking steps that would potentially help it acquire a nuke. A former al-Qaeda member once on the US terror list is now the US-backed ruler of Syria, warmly welcomed in Washington where the US commander who once fought him in Iraq gushed he was now a “fan.” And Washington is now flirting with normalizing relations with the Taliban, whose connections to that same al-Qaeda set the stage for two decades of war in Afghanistan that ended with the group back in charge of the country.The war on terror has become a zombie, devoid of everything that gave it life in the first place but more dangerous than ever, marching endlessly, mindlessly on in search of new living flesh to devour. It turns out this is, tragically, the legacy of that terrible day. We’ve forgotten why 9/11 happened, who perpetrated it, what lessons we should have learned. But the monster we unleashed simply lumbers on and on, the power to stop it seemingly out of anyone’s hands.

articles.title: Why Is It So Hard to Imagine the End of American Empire?
articles.author: Daniel Bessner
articles.content: The September 11, 2001, attacks on New York City and Washington, DC, as the saying goes, “changed everything.” After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the global American empire, created in the 1940s to combat communism, was left without a raison d’être . While foreign policymakers spent the 1990s searching for one, the best they could come up with — use the military power of the United States to stop humanitarian abuses abroad — was quixotic at best, catastrophic at worst. For a time, the empire lost its juice. The attacks changed all that. After 9/11, the United States identified a new global mission: fight “jihadist terrorism” wherever it might be found. We all know how that turned out. The United States lurched from disaster to disaster, killing and deracinating millions of people abroad. And at home, the so-called global war on terror (GWOT) engendered police militarization, polarization, and cynicism. Today few Americans deny that we live in an empire. But why has there been so little opposition to it? To answer this question, I’ve written a book , Imperialist Realism: Politics and Culture at the End of the American Century , an excerpt from which is printed below. Building on Mark Fisher’s concept of “capitalist realism,” I introduce the concept of “imperialist realism” — the notion that it is easier to imagine the end of the world than it is to imagine the end of the US empire. Americans have become alienated from our empire. We feel as though it’s outside our control even as we deploy its influence, money, and weapons abroad. The apparently obdurate character of our empire is the primary reason Americans accept it. The muted response to 9/11’s twenty-fifth anniversary is one sign among many that Americans have lost our zeal for empire. But our apathy presents an opportunity: we can overcome imperialist realism and finally end the world 9/11 created. But to do so, we must first understand how imperialist realism came to be. The End of Mass Politics and the Failure of the Global War on Terror Imperialist realism is a function of several structuring conditions. The most basic of these is the fact that, since the early 1940s, US elites have sought global military and economic primacy. Nevertheless, the pursuit of primacy is a necessary but not sufficient condition for imperialist realism’s emergence. Imperialist realism became the common sense of an era as the result of two other factors: first, the end of mass politics, and second, the failure of the global war on terror. Genuinely mass politics is a relatively recent phenomenon. Beginning in the nineteenth century and continuing into the twentieth, intertwined processes of urbanization, industrialization, and technological development reshaped politics across the North Atlantic world, giving ordinary people more power than they ever had before. In effect, as people moved from rural areas to cities, became industrial wage workers, and organized in unions, and as new technologies such as the telegraph and radio enabled leaders to communicate directly with large groups of citizens, a novel type of political formation — the “mass public,” which was considered to have an “opinion” — arose. For the first time in history, government officials started to conclude that their policies needed to have some relationship to what the mass public desired. Predictably, the emergence of the mass public as a political force engendered significant discussion among intellectuals about the proper role “public opinion” should play in policymaking. In the 1920s United States, two prominent thinkers, the journalist Walter Lippmann and the philosopher John Dewey, engaged in a debate that continues to define how American elites understand the public’s political function. On one side, Lippmann argued that ordinary people were simply too ignorant and too easily manipulated to be given the reins of public policy. In place of the public, Lippmann affirmed that social scientists needed to attach themselves to institutions that directly provided the government with advice. Lippmann thus presented technical expertise as the solution to the problem of mass politics. On the other side, Dewey averred that, though Lippmann was correct to doubt the public’s wisdom, elites should not ignore the masses but must instead educate them. Through education, Dewey claimed, ordinary people could eventually gain the knowledge necessary to make astute political choices. Initially, most American intellectuals embraced Dewey’s position over Lippmann’s: democracy, they maintained, relied on an educated mass public. Nevertheless, by the late 1930s, historical events in the United States and abroad led many thinkers to change their minds and endorse Lippmann over Dewey. First, the Great Depression, which witnessed bank runs, labor militancy, and other “irrational” mass behaviors, suggested to many intellectuals that the public was innately unreasonable. Second, and more important, the ascendance in Germany of the Nazi Party — whose power, Americans believed, rested on the masses — demonstrated to many observers that ordinary people could easily be duped to support destructive dictators such as Adolf Hitler. Together, the domestic responses to the Great Depression and the rise of Nazism persuaded an emergent majority of American elites that the masses could not be trusted. Mass politics and public opinion became things to be tamed and manipulated rather than improved. The stakes of the debate over public opinion became especially high during and after World War II. Following the fall of France in the summer of 1940, American elites concluded that the future of their nation, “Western civilization,” and humanity as a whole depended on the United States’ triumphing over Nazi Germany, a country whose fascist politics represented an illiberal attempt to address the problems of mass industrial society. In essence, US elites began viewing international relations as a sphere of life defined by a zero-sum struggle between Manichaean enemies, the winner of which would determine the fate of the world. Luckily for those who endorsed this position, the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor and other US-controlled territories in December 1941 made it easy for the United States to go to war; in the days after the attack, 97 percent of Americans approved Congress’s declaring war against Japan, and 91 percent said that President Franklin Delano Roosevelt should have also asked Congress to declare war on Germany. For the remainder of World War II, most Americans accepted that their country needed to defeat the Axis. The situation, however, was not so simple in the early Cold War. While, after World War II, manifold American elites rapidly transferred their anxieties about Hitler and Nazism onto Joseph Stalin, Bolshevism, and “international communism” writ large, they didn’t trust that the public — which, they worried, had proven itself ignorant and capricious in the past — would necessarily do the same. Indeed, as late as May 1947, 35 percent of Americans said they had “friendly” “feelings” toward Russia (i.e., the Soviet Union). This presented elites with a problem: How could they ensure that the irrational mass public would allow its leaders to prosecute a potentially decades-long “cold war” against the Soviet Union, a nation that had only recently been an ally? American elites developed a clever solution to their conundrum: to guarantee that ordinary people didn’t stand in the way of the Cold War, they constructed a governance apparatus designed to limit the public’s impact on foreign policy. The creation of executive branch groups such as the National Security Council, the Central Intelligence Agency, and the Department of Defense, as well as parastatal organizations such as the RAND Corporation and other national security–focused think tanks and academic centers, institutionalized a system in which elites, not the masses, made the important foreign policy decisions. Put another way, in the late 1940s the United States embraced two distinct “containment” policies. Internationally, US elites sought to contain the Soviet Union by preventing it from improving its global power position; domestically, they sought to contain the American public by preventing it from shaping US foreign policy. From its inception, the US pursuit of global primacy was accompanied by a domestic democratic deficit. Since World War II, the public has had at best a minor influence on the conception and execution of US foreign policy. All the major strategic decisions made by US elites after 1945 — to spend an enormous amount on the military; to build a global empire of bases; to deploy hundreds of thousands of troops abroad; to intervene repeatedly in the politics and economies of other countries — have been made with only passing reference to public opinion. This is not to say that American politicians and officials have always ignored the public; they’ve often paid attention to and tried to manipulate it. Still, the public was rarely, if ever, the driver of US foreign policy. Even Congress, the institutional representative of the people’s will, has been a secondary player in US foreign policy and war-making. Indeed, the last time Congress declared war was on June 4, 1942, against Bulgaria, Hungary, and Romania despite the fact that, as the political scientists Monica Duffy Toft and Sidita Kushi have discovered, between 1946 and 2019 the United States intervened abroad with “the threat, display, or direct usage of force” 216 times. Though the language of mass politics continues to permeate US discourse and influence how Americans conceive of their political role, when it comes to foreign policy, we do not live in a mass democracy and haven’t for almost a century. The powerlessness of the masses in the realm of foreign affairs is one of the two key structuring conditions that make imperialist realism possible. While the organizations and practices of the age of mass politics remain extant — Americans still vote for mass political parties; we still engage with politics through mass media; we still participate in mass protests — these are not effective vehicles for the will of the demos. Ours is an individualistic, atomized, and alienated era overlaid with atavistic institutions unable to influence the power elite. Indeed, research suggests that wealthy capitalists are the only people capable of shaping policy. According to the political scientists Martin Gilens and Benjamin I. Page, “multivariate analysis indicates that economic elites and organized groups representing business interests have substantial independent impacts on U.S. government policy, while average citizens and mass-based interest groups have little or no independent influence.” Is it any surprise that Americans have become cynical about politics? In fact, a recent report by NORC at the University of Chicago revealed that, when polled, “barely one in ten Americans thought the government represents them well”; 70 percent “thought politicians were only out for themselves”; and just 19 percent “said people in government could be trusted to do what’s right.” The other necessary condition for imperialist realism’s emergence is more proximate: the failure of the global war on terror. For those who don’t remember the early 2000s, it’s difficult to overstate how patriotic, jingoistic, and — importantly — hopeful Americans became once the George W. Bush Administration committed the United States to fighting a war on “terror.” In January 2002, for example, 93 percent of Americans believed that the United States made the correct decision to send military forces to Afghanistan and 66 percent said the United States was “winning the war against terrorism.” To many Americans, the GWOT was a world-historical project that united the country in a moment when the United States lacked an existential enemy and thus lacked an organizing principle for both domestic life and US foreign policy. This conviction was perhaps best reflected in Bush’s 2002 State of the Union address, in which the president declared that the 2000s “will be a decisive decade in the history of liberty” because Americans have “been called to a unique role in human events” — to eliminate “terrorists” and all those who supported them. But the GWOT did not proceed as planned. Instead of marching to triumph, the United States lurched from disaster to disaster. Above all, Americans fought, and lost, a twenty-year war in Afghanistan and an eight-year war in Iraq. The GWOT, which expanded beyond Afghanistan and Iraq to Pakistan, Syria, and other countries, cost around $8 trillion, engendered the displacement of thirty-eight million people, resulted in at least 940,000 direct deaths and 3.6–3.8 million indirect deaths, witnessed the deaths of over seven thousand US troops, and helped impel police militarization, political polarization, and the erosion of civil liberties at home. Without putting too fine a point on it, the GWOT was one of the most significant failures in the history of US foreign relations: the disconnect between the hopes placed in the GWOT and its vicious, violent, and counterproductive reality undermined Americans’ belief in themselves and their country. Because of it, the United States is a more cynical place.

articles.title: How The War on Terror Continues To Terrorize Communities 25 Years Later
articles.content: In early 2025 , the world watched as masked federal agents abducted Pro-Palestinian activists across the country based on the premise that they were promoting or supporting terrorism. Having tested various legal boundaries through these cases, the Trump administration became further emboldened later that year, issuing the National Security Presidential Memorandum (NSPM- 7 ) in September 2025 . The memorandum effectively equated certain political and ideological beliefs with terrorism, and a slew of politically motivated attacks quickly followed. In June 2026 , the Justice Department indicted two Cop City activists in Georgia on arson charges. Within the same week, charges were brought against eight pro-Palestine activists in Michigan and 15 anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activists in Minnesota . Although these attacks have in many ways felt unprecedented, they must be seen as a continuation of the War on Terror, in which the security apparatus constructed over the last 25 years is now being used to aggressively target political dissent within the United States. Issued less than a year into President Trump’s term, NSPM- 7 broadens an already elusive definition of terrorism, declaring differing ideological beliefs as indicators of violence. Specifically, the memorandum links ​ “ anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, anti-Christianity, support for the overthrow of the United States government; extremism on migration, race, and gender; and hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality” with a propensity for violent conduct. Based on this purported likelihood of committing domestic terrorist acts, the memorandum authorizes law enforcement to preemptively target individuals before and after ​ “ violent” political acts occur. Since the issuance of NSPM- 7 , activists on the political Left have been routinely targeted, from the Prairieland defendants who have received a combined sentence of over 556 years in prison for an anti-ICE demonstration the administration labeled a ​ “ terrorist attack,” to the range of Cuba solidarity activists whom the U.S. State Department has labeled as ​ “ terrorists” to justify further attacks. The issuance of NSPM- 7 and the accompanying attacks have only been made possible because of the legal frameworks and erosion of legal safeguards that have accompanied 25 years of the so-called War on Terror. For example, the NSPM- 7 relies on the concept of preventative policing, which was popularized in the aftermath of the September 11 , 2001 attacks. Government programs like the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System (NSEERS) and Countering Violent Extremism were premised on this very idea, where religious and national identity served as a supposed precursor to ​ “ terrorist activity.” These programs expanded state power while routinely curtailing individuals’ fundamental rights through mass surveillance of communities, the expansion of material support of terrorism laws, and the detention and torture of countless individuals. Despite the documented, widespread human rights abuses such government programs resulted in, the lack of domestic and global accountability have allowed the preventative policing model to resurface through NSPM- 7 , this time with a focus on left-leaning groups. The administration’s recent efforts to silence dissent in Minnesota as part of its campaign to target ​ “ domestic terrorism” serve as one recent example. There, undercover federal agents launched surveillance programs to infiltrate and monitor left-leaning groups, including labor unions, political organizations, and activists, among others. While Operation Puppet Master authorized spying on community members, Project Whipple Shield aimed to identify organizing efforts that disrupted federal activities. Both investigations authorized mass surveillance of certain left-leaning groups based on the premise that activists were aiding ​ “ violent opportunists and agitators, ” similar to the logic adopted by the preventative policing model. The legal framework of the ​ “ War on Terror” has influenced NSPM- 7 in many other ways as well. The USA Patriot Act, also passed after September 11 , 2001 , included a definition of ​ “ domestic terrorism” that human rights groups warned could subject political organizations to surveillance and criminal charges. As these groups predicted, NSPM- 7 relies on the already elusive definition in the Patriot Act to categorize dissent as ​ “ terrorist activity.” NSPM- 7 simultaneously builds on the Patriot Act’s expansion of ​ “ material support to terrorism” laws outlined in two U.S. statutes, 18 U.S.C. § 2339 A and § 2339 B. While Section 2339 A targets those who provide material support or resources for any offense identified as a federal crime of terrorism, Section 2339 B applies to those who provide material support or resources to a ​ “ foreign terrorist organization,” as designated by the U.S. State Department. From reliance on preventative policing to inclusion of provisions of the USA Patriot Act, NSPM- 7 cannot be separated from the War on Terror that has plagued our communities for over two decades. Alarmingly, the impacts of the War on Terror on the current crackdown on dissent are felt not only at the federal level but also at the state level as well, where the administration and its allies are building legal infrastructure to expand their attacks on dissent. In addition to NSPM- 7 , states like Florida have passed legislation that leverages the power of the state to instill fear and crush political dissent in movement and organizing groups. Specifically, House Bill 1471 in Florida, which came into effect in July 2026 , gives state officials the power to designate organizations as ​ “ domestic terrorists.” House Bill 1473 then prohibits organizations from accessing records related to that designation, limiting the ability for impacted organizations to challenge such designations. States like Georgia have already followed suit and attempted to pass similar legislation. As the United States continues to expand on the ​ “ terrorism” framework and wage a so-called ​ “ War on Terror,” the country’s approach to terrorism is being exported globally. With facism on the rise in various countries, authoritarian leaders continue to look for ways to silence political ideologies that threaten the status quo. Following President Trump’s attacks on pro-Palestinian solidarity activists, the United Kingdom voted to ban Palestine Action under the country’s terrorism laws, an organization that seeks to take direct action to end ​ “ global complicity with Israel’s genocidal apartheid regime.” As a result, four activists were sentenced with terrorism enhancements for their involvement in a protest and raid at an arms manufacturer for Israel, despite the fact that they themselves were not convicted of terrorism. The UK joins a growing list of countries like India , which have long abused counterterrorism measures to silence dissent. The United States itself is also making strides to ensure that its policies are adopted elsewhere, recently hosting a conference for over 65 countries to discuss the ​ “ Resurgence of Political Terrorism .” The conference discussed three kinds of threats, including ​ “ violent left-wing extremists,” with the hopes of expanding coordination and information sharing between countries. Given the United States’ increased McCarthyite targeting of political dissenters, including individuals and organizations who have spoken out about the inhumane U.S. blockade on Cuba , serious concerns remain regarding what oppressive frameworks other countries will adopt to silence political dissent as the United States continues to test legal limits. While the latest actions of the Trump administration feel unprecedented, the War on Terror is anything but new for the communities who have faced its devastating impacts. For the last 25 years, activists and community members alike have raised alarms, arguing that the systems expanding the national security apparatus to target ​ “ terrorism” were not only resulting in present harm but held future terrifying ramifications — much like the ones we are experiencing today. It is well past time that we take heed of their warnings, deconstruct the ​ “ terrorism” apparatus, and put forward new frameworks that collectively protect our fundamental rights.

articles.title: 25 Years After 9/11, How Do We Build a Movement To Stop Forever Wars?
articles.content: The Twin Towers of the World Trade Center emit smoke on Sept. 11, 2001. (WIKIMEDIA) Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11 , 2001 , on the surface it may seem that American foreign policy has followed a course filled with continuity. A quarter century ago, the United States launched the ​ “ War on Terror” in response to 9 / 11 . Today, President Donald Trump’s attacks on Iran have embroiled the country in another conflict in the Middle East. Yet while the War on Terror gave rise to a disastrous wave of military intervention, it also produced a historic surge of antiwar activism, which played a critical role in discrediting ​ “ forever wars” across the political spectrum. Whereas the Iraq War began with 70 % public approval, Trump’s war in Iran has been widely opposed from the beginning, with only around a third of Americans currently in support . Jeremy Varon, a historian at the New School for Social Research, recently released the first definitive history of antiwar organizing against the War on Terror. His book is entitled Our Grief Is Not a Cry for War . I spoke with Varon to discuss the organizing that took place against the war in Iraq that started in 2003 , the impact the movement had, and how that activism has been popularly remembered — or, too often, forgotten. We also discussed the prospects for antiwar organizing today, when Trump’s attacks on Iran are wildly unpopular, and yet we lack a movement that can be a mechanism for raising the political costs of interventionism. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity. There is a very common impression — maybe the dominant impression of antiwar activism under George W. Bush — that the movement was a failure because it did not stop the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003 . I think that is a distorted perception of the impact the movement did have. What is your assessment? The first thing to say is that success and failure are relative. And indeed, certainly with regard to the invasion of Iraq, the movement failed in its overarching goal to stop the war before it started. A lot of people intuitively knew that when the bombs started falling, disaster would follow, and that reorienting American policy would be like turning around a tanker, not a tugboat. If you look at American military casualties, the implosion of Iraqi society, civilian casualties and so on, the calamity that people feared came to pass. I can appreciate the sense of failure many activists felt, because the stakes were so high — literally life and death. That said, the antiwar movement can claim accomplishments as well. It substantially delegitimated the war before it ever started, especially within the realms of global public opinion and even geopolitics. The United States went to war with just one significant military and political ally: the United Kingdom. It didn’t have the support of traditional allies in Western Europe, like France and Germany. Most of Latin America, Asia and Central Europe rejected the U.S. position. The United Nations, while not declaring the war illegal, fundamentally disapproved of it, and Secretary General Kofi Annan privately thought the war would be a grave mistake. So the actual military campaign was inhibited by both a domestic and a global movement arguing that the war was wrong-headed and likely illegal. In a way, the antiwar movement peaked before the Iraq War even started. On February 15 , 2003 , you had thousands of coordinated antiwar protests all over the world. Between 15 and 30 million people turned out to protest the war. It was the largest single day of protest in human history. For sure, many people on the streets that day were gravely disappointed that the demonstration didn’t have the intended effect of preventing the war. Some percentage maybe never came back to the antiwar movement, because they were so dispirited. But organizing the mass demonstrations built a protest infrastructure that lived on. The main antiwar coalition in the U.S. came into its own through those demonstrations. I give enormous credit to the people who had the tenacity and stamina to keep grinding away at protest. I’m thinking of Code Pink, United for Peace and Justice, World Can’t Wait and all of these smaller grassroots formations throughout the country that continued to organize. When the war started, public opinion in the U.S. was substantially in its favor, around 70 % right after the ​ “ shock and awe” invasion. But that was a soft 70 %, with people in the middle rallying around the flag. They wanted the swift victory Bush promised, which would mean limited American casualties. But as the war bogged down, the antiwar position grew steadily more salient, and antiwar sentiment grew steadily bigger. Eventually, public opinion caught up with the antiwar movement. The most recent polling is from 2023 or so. Something like 60 % of the American public, by that point, thought that the Iraq War was a mistake. A similar percentage thought the Afghanistan War, long considered the ​ “ good war,” was a mistake. And a whopping 58 % of veterans of both deployments think that the wars were not worth fighting. We’ll never know with any certainty the extent to which the war itself or the antiwar movement was the driver of shifts in public opinion. But in my book I cite observers who argue that the antiwar movement likely limited the duration and intensity of the war in Iraq, and therefore saved lives. That’s a highly general statement, but I think it’s a fair statement. Others note that it may have constrained the neoconservatives in the George W. Bush administration from pursuing military action in places like Iran and Syria, which had very much been on their agenda. In the book you write that, as the Bush administration launched its invasion of Iraq in 2003 , ​ “ For months, the public had been schooled in the reasons for the invasion, and expectations for it. Americans were also versed, if to a lesser degree, in the case against the war. Events on the ground would determine which position was right.” I think that’s a very important point: In relation to the War on Terror, the movement created a counter-narrative about what the administration was doing and what actions were actually going to make us safer. And so when the war started going bad, there was already an explanation in place for why this was always a horrible idea and why there should be political consequences. Yes, and this is important for understanding how public discourse and policy interrelate. There was a counter-narrative about the war coming from the movement. It said that Iraq doesn’t pose a clear and present danger, that there’s no proof of the existence of weapons of mass destruction, that lots of people are going to die, and that it may plunge the region into chaos. Over time, more and more observers could see the reality aligning with those warnings. Rather than having to create arguments against the war from scratch, people who were growing increasingly critical could appeal to an existing body of antiwar criticisms and bring them into the public square in a new way. Eventually, you have the political class catching up with where the public already was — aligned, more or less, with the core positions of an antiwar movement. It’s a long and complex process by which dissenting ideas achieve a kind of hegemony and then compel shifts in policy. Even endless wars can end, when they lose legitimacy in the eyes of the nation waging them. That process begins at the grassroots. Of course, the end of the war came too late to spare untold death and destruction. But the antiwar movement at least limited the damage, and that’s a real achievement. One of the ways in which the antiwar movement had a swifter impact was in shifting the debate within the Democratic Party. You quickly go from having the leadership of the party voting in favor of the war in Iraq, to there being a complete revolt from the base. This results in the rise of figures such as antiwar candidate Howard Dean in 2004 , and it leads to the eventual Democratic nominee John Kerry trying to position himself as an antiwar candidate — even though he’s not an entirely credible one. In the 2004 election, George W. Bush was an incumbent, wartime president who most analysts expected to coast to victory based on the massive surge of patriotism after 9 / 11 . And instead this election, in no small part, became a referendum on the war and became an extremely close race. If just 60 , 000 votes in Ohio had gone the other way, Bush would have been ousted. During the electoral season in 2004 , much of the antiwar movement considered Bush’s defeat to be the quickest way to end the war. The war had already started to crash and burn, but ultimately not badly enough to turn the tide against Bush. Remarkably, he won the so-called ​ “ security vote.” Bush had gifted political operatives, notably Karl Rove, who had him run on culture war issues and turned out droves of evangelicals. Last, there was an enormous effort by the right to discredit John Kerry over his opposition to the Vietnam War. As it is, he was a kind of wishy-washy alternative on the war in Iraq, whom the antiwar movement only grudgingly backed. It ended up being a close election. Bush’s win was a huge disappointment, even a shock for progressives. Still, the antiwar movement found a way to write another chapter. By late 2005 , the failures of the Iraq War — along with the callousness of the administration’s response to Hurricane Katrina — had turned George W. Bush into a premature lame duck president, hamstringing him for the rest of his second term. I would argue that antiwar activism played a big role in that. What is your take? After the 2004 elections, a new wave of antiwar activism emerges, with powerful new advocates and constituencies. With Cindy Sheehan, most famously, it had a grieving Gold Star mother asking, ​ “ For what noble cause did my son die?” She was really asking, for Bush and the nation to hear, why the war was being fought at all. For weeks in the summer of 2005 , Cindy Sheehan and others set up Camp Casey — named after her son — near Bush’s ranch in Texas. Veterans, antiwar activists, celebrities, everyday people and important politicians all gravitated to it. It became ground zero, if you will, for the antiwar movement. And it got intense coverage: CNN, Anderson Cooper, Oprah Winfrey and all sorts of global media. It was the first time since the big demonstrations in 2003 that the antiwar movement drove the narrative. For millions of Americans, the suffering and folly of the war felt real in a new way. From the start, some families of 9 / 11 victims had opposed war, and their voices had unique power. You also had groups like Veterans for Peace working to communicate the bitter lessons of Vietnam to the American public. By 2005 , they were joined by a growing mass of veterans of the Iraq War, and even active duty soldiers, reporting that American conduct had nothing to do with spreading peace and freedom and democracy. Instead, it was menacing Iraqis and turning the Iraqi people against the occupation. They had seen it themselves. With the activism of the military community, the antiwar movement took on a somewhat different class character. Sheehan is a kind of upper-working-class, all-American mom from small town California, and veterans typically hail from the working class. The U.S. military is a working-class institution. It is also racially a very integrated institution. So you have heartland spokespeople, speaking from a heartland perspective, denouncing a war that is chewing up their lives and falling far short of the high-minded ambitions that Bush had set for it. And I think this gives a kind of permission structure for everyday Americans, who may consider themselves conventionally patriotic, to say, ​ “ Wait a second. Who is this war helping?” Then Hurricane Katrina hits in late August. The botched response is a massive policy failure for the Bush administration, which claimed it had things under control. The whole nation could see that was a lie. Camp Casey breaks up, with a whole contingent, led by Veterans for Peace, leaving Crawford, Texas and rushing to New Orleans. In and around the city, they distribute massive amounts of food, water and other necessities. They use satellite phones to help the Red Cross save people from rooftops. They help people get legal services and deal with insurance companies. They felt duty-bound to rally to the suffering present in America. And they absolutely made the connection of the misuse of resources to wage a foreign war that the country no longer wanted with the neglect of urgent problems at home. Then, in September, a pre-planned demonstration happens in Washington that very much connects conditions at home and overseas. It was in some ways the most ambitious of all the antiwar protests — three days that included lobbying, civil disobedience, art exhibits, interfaith events and on-the-ground organizing. From 2006 on, you have the painful extrication of the United States from a quagmire of its own making. By late 2005 , you see a cratering of public opinion in support of the war. And the pro-war stance never again becomes the majority position. Soon enough, you have powerful people in Congress giving new credibility to the antiwar position. There was the famous ​ “ Murthquake,” in which John Murtha, a military veteran and initially a big supporter of the war, comes out against it. He himself said that the political class was way behind public opinion. And then you have the 2006 midterms, where this sentiment is translated into a major defeat for the Republicans. Yes. The Democrats have blowout wins, functionally retaking control of both houses of Congress based on an antiwar message. After that it was really a question of when and not if the war ends, with the U.S. far short of having achieved the military and geostrategic objectives that Bush set. From 2006 on, you have the painful extrication of the United States from a quagmire of its own making. What I consider the most significant Congressional action after 2006 was the impaneling of the Iraq Study Group. That was a bipartisan group to diagnose what went wrong and advocate a way forward, which was ultimately some form of U.S. withdrawal. You have the eminences of the American foreign policy establishment basically calling bullshit on Bush’s signature policy. When they release their report, it’s a bestseller. It’s being sold in bookstores and airports and downloaded something like two million times. Reading the narrative you present in your book, and remembering all of the organizing that took place on so many different fronts, it’s startling how much of it has been utterly forgotten in the media and in the popular imagination. What do you think accounts for that? The movement, in its own day, was woefully underreported on. I blame the legacy media and major cable outfits — almost all of the press, really — for confusing post- 9 / 11 patriotism with an excuse to abdicate its responsibility to report on domestic dissent. For years, activists struggled to get sustained attention to their efforts. I was part of this movement, but probably 90 percent of what I report on in my book, I had no idea was happening at the time. Part of the intent of the book is to give this big, robust, spirited, movement its due, while also understanding why knowledge about it was suppressed. The larger purpose is to try to induce a broader legal, political and moral reckoning with the totality of the War on Terror. My argument is that we hear so little about the antiwar movement in part because we hear so little about the War on Terror itself. It’s as though the Iraq War never happened. It was so consequential, it was so costly in blood and treasure. But, historically speaking, it feels almost like a non-event. My college students know almost nothing about it. I was born in 1967 , and I came of age in the post-Vietnam War era. That war had a massive, lasting impact on American political life and culture. There was the ​ “ Vietnam Syndrome” that discouraged new wars. There was the Vietnam Veterans War Memorial in Washington. Every Hollywood auteur made a Vietnam War movie. It was understood that the United States had been through something big and traumatic, and that the nation needed soul-searching to examine its foreign policy, the meaning of patriotism and the appropriate uses of the military. The War on Terror, in its most intense phase, has not been succeeded by anything like that kind of public reflection. We badly need it. My thesis is that the War on Terror was so ugly, so confusing, so divisive, that we simply don’t know what to do with it. And when you don’t know what to do with something, the easiest thing is to ignore it. Of course, there are millions of people for whom forgetting isn’t a luxury: all the Iraqis who were murdered or displaced or dismembered, and all these veterans suffering from traumatic head wounds or who have missing limbs. We owe it to them to remember and learn from past mistakes. Today, we face a unique situation in that Trump’s war in Iran is incredibly unpopular, and across political parties there is huge opposition to the U.S. getting into so-called ​ “ forever wars.” And yet, we lack any large antiwar movement that is actively raising the political cost of unpopular interventionism. It’s stunning. My take is that Trump doesn’t like ​ “ endless wars” for all of the obvious reasons. At the same time, he is eager to use the lethality of the American military to project his own power on the global stage. For him, stupid wars are simply wars that the United States can’t easily win. So he craves ​ “ victory.” He got very excited by the intervention in Venezuela and the initial strikes against Iran. And he thought that, with advances in military technology, we could have these quick-hit mini-victories with minimal, if not negligible, cost in American lives. Right now, we’re in this weird limbo with the Iran conflict . On the one hand, it’s a war frightfully outside traditional constraints on a president, which Trump disdains. He doesn’t believe in limits set by Congress, international law, the U.N., or the opinions of allies. At the same time, he likely recognizes that some number of U.S. casualties would be unacceptible to Americans and would sink the war. So that lesson from Iraq, from Vietnam even, he does seem to get. My fear is that low-intensity conflicts, like in Iran, may grow routine and become background noise in American political life that never quite rile the public to demand their end. The trick for Trump is to continue waging war without prohibitive costs that would trigger widespread outrage among a disapproving but disaffected public. I think the midterms will be a crucial test of whether disapproving public opinion can have a real price. If the Democrats win big, we may have part of the answer. I would love it if there were a dedicated antiwar movement addressing Iran as well as possible intervention in Cuba. Personally, I don’t think we’re going to have such a movement. Barring some dramatic escalation of the war in Iran, which is still possible, I think we’re going to have a continuation of the current circumstance where dissatisfaction with the war is one of a number of grievances with Trump — along with the public corruption, inattention to issues of affordability, vanity projects, et cetera. If Republicans get routed, public opinion experts will have to sift through the data to find out how important the war has been. What lessons do you draw from antiwar organizing in the years after 9 / 11 that you think are relevant for movements today? I think there are strategic lessons for activists today. One is that, while a movement’s message matters, the messenger matters enormously as well. When it’s a Gold Star mother, when it’s a veteran, when it’s an ex-general, when it’s a formerly pro-war politician articulating an antiwar position, the message behaves very differently than it might otherwise. Effective movements always need to think about how to present and highlight those voices that have the greatest credibility among the broader public and political class. We may bristle at this dynamic, but historically our most successful social movements have understood that. Another takeaway is the general power of conscientious dissent to alter political conditions. If you think of Bush declaring ​ “ Mission Accomplished,” which he did on May 1 , 2003 , it was a great moment of bluster. But then you look at the profound turning of the American public on the War on Terror over the two years that followed. It’s a remarkable difference. That change would have been incredibly hard to predict. That’s part of political life and part of life more generally. We can be thoughtful, we can be strategic, we can identify goals, but we can’t ultimately know the consequences of our actions in advance. America and the world would have been much better off if antiwar voices had genuinely been listened to, and not belittled and ignored. People with enormous expertise and good moral instincts captured the truth of the moment. So one needs to work really hard — against the biases of the media and government alike — to make one’s truth heard. There are rewards of stamina, even when things seem bleak. Any number of issues, from global warming, to Gaza, to the abuses of immigrants, feel incredibly bleak now. But temporary setbacks shouldn’t be a reason for resignation. History has too many examples of the rewards of holding on to hope. This story was also posted at Waging Nonviolence .
